status: agreed text of two independent transcriptions (Claude, workflow 2026-10-27; GPT-6 Astra, Codex 2026-10-27); every difference decided against the scans by two anonymised checkers (2026-10-27), places they left open by the editor
conventions: diplomatic, as printed: long s -> s; ligatures resolved; abbreviations expanded silently (& -> et, nasal stroke -> m/n); the q-acute sort kept as q́ue; u/v, i/j, accents, capitals and misprints as printed; printed hyphens kept; spacing normalised as in the merged Xylander (no space before punctuation, one after)

differences.reason: A: 1 (medium) — The glyph is a serifed upright 'I' shape, a little top-heavy, followed by a point. It matches exactly this font's figure one, as in the page number '41' and the '1' of the scale diagram on p.44. The other chapter headings use Arabic figures: 'CAPVT 3.' on p.44, 'CAP. 4.' on p.50, 'CAPVT 5.' on p.51. So this is the old-style figure 1, not a Roman numeral, but the shape alone cannot tell the two apart. | B: 1 (medium) — The numeral is an upright stroke at small-cap height with top and bottom serifs, and the top serif hooks slightly left. It has the same shape as the arabic old-style '1' in the page number '41' and in the marginal paragraph number, so its shape alone cannot settle 1 vs I. The other chapter headings in this set use arabic numerals (p.44 'CAPVT 3.', p.50 'CAP. 4.', p.51 'CAPVT 5.'), so arabic 1 is the probable reading.

A: convention (high) — Comma set tight against 'i' with no word space ('portio,ipsa…'). Only the space differs here; the accent is dealt with under difference 2. | B: convention (high) — No space after the comma. 'portio,' is set tight against 'ipſ' (8x crop). This is only a difference in spacing after punctuation.

A: 2 (high) — At 8x and 14x, plus a pixel map: the 'a' (x 283-299) has nothing above it. A short acute stroke rising to the right (x 309-316, y 1160-1163) stands over the bowl of the following 'q' (x 304-324). So the print has ipsaq́ue, the enclitic mark on q, not ipsáque. Under the q́ue = que convention this gives 'ipsaque'. | B: 2 (high) — At 10x the 'a' of ipſa has no accent. A short acute stroke stands over the bowl of the q, i.e. the q-acute sort (ipſaq́ue). By the conventions q́ue is silently 'que', so 'ipsaque' is right. 'ipsáque' puts an accent on the a that is not printed.

figures.description: Line diagram of a divided string: a horizontal line from A (left end) to B (right end), with short vertical I-shaped ticks. Arabic numbers above, letters below, read left to right: tick at A under the number 9; then a cluster of three close ticks lettered M, I, L (8 stands over L; M nearest A, I in the middle); then ticks lettered K (7), H (6), G (5), F (4), E (3), D (2; the letter is an odd, rotated-looking glyph, probably a damaged or turned D), C (1); then a short segment to a tick at B. So the points C-L stand at equal steps 1-8 from the B end, A at 9, and M and I divide the last step L-A (I nearer L, M nearer A), illustrating the semitone (8 1/2) and diesis (8 1/4) of the text. The small middle letter of the cluster may be read T.

figures.description: Woodcut line diagram for the ratios 4:3, 3:2 and 2:1: three pairs of parallel horizontal lines, with capital letters at the ends and at the division ticks and small numerals under some segments. Pair 1: upper line A-B (A at left, B at the right end-stroke), divided by three ticks labelled above C, a letter shaped like a reversed D (probably D), and E; the numeral 4 stands under the segment E-B. Lower line from a second reversed-D-shaped letter at the left to F, which stands directly under E; it has ticks under C and under the first reversed D, labelled below I and K. Pair 2: upper line L-N (end-stroke before N), divided by two ticks labelled above P and Y (Y preceded by a stray capital B, printed 'BY'); the numeral 3 stands under the segment Y-N. Lower line M-o (M at left with end-stroke, small o after the right end-stroke under Y), with one tick under P labelled below R; the numeral 2 stands below this line between R and o, immediately above the Z of pair 3. Pair 3: upper line S-V (end-strokes at both ends) with one tick in the middle labelled Z above; the numeral 2 under the segment Z-V. Lower line T-X ending under Z, with the numeral 1 under it. The pairs show 4 parts against 3, 3 against 2 and 2 against 1 (sesquitertius, sesquialter, duplex).

alignment_with_xylander_gpt.remark: Ends at «largitur» in Xyl. 41.1. Vinet combines the universe/music exposition that Xylander divides into two indented paragraphs.
Begins at «nos de ea Musica» within Xyl. 41.1. The restriction to audible music is a separate numbered paragraph in Vinet.
Ends at «usui» in Xyl. 41.16. Definitions of sound, interval, system and harmony, followed by the requirement of consonance.
Begins at «Proinde» and ends with the last note name «hyperbolæon». Vinet sets the fifteen names on separate lines; Xylander prints a continuous list. «Mése solùm» corresponds to «mese monos».

Begins at «Per has». Both descriptions combine a sixteen-string designation with a fifteen-string instrument and the shared eighth note; neither numerical wording has been emended merely to harmonise them.

Ends at «minui» before «Id uerò». Vinet expresses the semitone and diesis as eight-and-a-half and eight-and-a-quarter; Xylander uses half and quarter of the sesquioctave. Vinet alone supplies the subdivided-line diagram after 44.12.

From «Id uerò in Arithmetica» to «duo sit quadratus)». The sixteen/thirty-two example has corresponding dot arrays: printed on Vinet 46 before line1; the arrays in the right margin of Xyl.43 have uncertain origin (printed or manuscript).
From «At Geometriæ» to «in diesin». Vinet supplies a lettered geometrical construction before 46.1; Xylander has no corresponding printed lettered construction in the supplied pages.
Begins at «Eorundem». Vinet calls the ensuing intervals «simplicia»; Xylander calls them «Incomposita». Their explanations occupy the same position in the argument.
Xylander additionally gives current names quarta, quinta, octaua and equivalents for the compound intervals. The order of fourth, fifth, octave and compound intervals agrees.
Ends at «quasi contrà sonans». Xylander adds explanatory glosses «quasi iuxta sonans» and «quasi contrà sonans»; Vinet gives the technical names without those glosses.
From «Inter paraphonum» to «proportionaliter». Xylander also supplies the glosses «assonans et obsonans».
From «Cæterùm» to «non tamen consonantia». Tone, semitone and diesis considered individually.
From «Conficitur» through «Disdiapason, ex duodecim tonis». The interval totals occur in the same order.

From «Proportio» through «uiginti quatuor». Vinet explicitly includes the quadruple ratio in the initial list; Xylander gives it in the ensuing numerical example. Xylander specifies «super bipartiens tertias», whereas Vinet says «duas eius partes». Vinet alone adds the three pairs of lettered segments after 49.6.

From «At enim» through «reliquis existimandum est». The distinction between pitch ratios and counts of notes is common. For comparison with the third note, Xylander specifies «eum, eiusque bessem» where Vinet has «superpartiens».
From «Porrò hæ proportiones» through «spiritus». Discovery of ratios by string length, thickness, tension and weights, then wind instruments.

From «Porrò systematum» through «complectitur». Xylander spells out the string counts and adds the contemporary name «decimamquintam». Vinet explicitly names the compound intervals at 51.1–3 where Xylander refers to «ex his ipsis composita».
From «Inter systemata» through «intelliguntur». Material systems are distinguished from intervals considered apart from matter.
From «Harmoniæ proprium» through «cantus conflatur». Xylander includes a parenthetical explanation of melodia as cantus/cantilena and its modulation.

From «Neque tamen» through «nomen inuenit». The three genera are constructed in the same order. Vinet calls the chromatic genus sadder and more mournful than the preceding one; Xylander describes its greater efficacy in moving emotions and evoking grief.
From «Neque alia ratione» through «faciet». Extension of the tetrachord example to other systems.
From «Sanè» through «Plato quoque id receperit». Difficulty of the harmonic genus and the natural simplicity of the diatonic genus.

From «Verùm horum præterea» to the end of the body. Modes and kinds of song, then variations of performance. Xylander's «obliquioribus» corresponds here to Vinet's «lentioribus»; this lexical divergence is reported without deciding between them. Closing formulas are Xyl.49.25 and Vinet53.21.

The glyph is a serifed upright stroke of the same form as this font's Arabic figure one (as in the page number «41»), but the shape alone cannot distinguish 1 from I; 1 is supported by the Arabic figures of the other chapter headings («CAPVT 3.», «CAP. 4.», «CAPVT 5.»). Decided by both checkers (with medium confidence).
